topics.title: Numerical Concept 2: Surds
topics.subject: mathematics
outcomes: Use surds to represent roots that cannot be represented exactly as decimals. (k, u)
Manipulate and simplify expressions with surds. (u, s, v/a)

body.text: A surd is a root, like √2 or √3, that cannot be simplified to a whole number or an exact terminating/recurring decimal — its decimal goes on forever without repeating. Leaving an answer as a surd (e.g. √2) is more exact than rounding it to a decimal (1.41421...).
To simplify a surd, look for a square factor inside the root and pull out its square root. √12 = √(4x3) = √4 x √3 = 2√3, because 4 is the largest perfect-square factor of 12.

Surds combine like algebraic terms: only surds with the same number under the root can be added or subtracted directly. 2√3 + 5√3 = 7√3, but 2√3 + 5√2 cannot be simplified further since the numbers under the roots differ. Multiplying surds follows √a x √b = √(ab): √2 x √8 = √16 = 4.

A fraction with a surd in the denominator, like 1/√2, is usually rationalised by multiplying top and bottom by that surd: 1/√2 x √2/√2 = √2/2. This removes the surd from the denominator without changing the value of the fraction.
